Filed Sept 20th, 1912 Placed in Primary Jv. about 2 or 3 o'clock you thin girls has to go to court in town Mr. Tompkins to call Mrs. Millan Crazy book Annie Frank's letters Oct 11, 1918 My dearest loving honey bunch how are you getting along now days, say honey I am locked up again that makes me feel I have been locked up. I have been locked up at the city jail at Ellenberg too. I don't care how you please excuse my writing honey I am writing on the bed but couldn't hardly write though lay honey I was so glad to see you back the girls all say that you were so lonesome when your brothers left you but I guess you're not again when he is back. Say I had a good time at Ellen's here I wished you were there with me don't you show this to Andrew Barnity if you do you hate me now so long loony Excuse my fast hand writing so long from Annie 4 na - 17 Mr Leo Hammer Cushman School Tacoma Wash Box 157. City Jail My dearest loving Mrs. Pearlie how is the girl getting along now days say honey my pencil is pretty bum I can't hardly write with it I sent Mahama has my other one old Mahama any way lay Jane I am so hungry for bread and syrup now I just don't know what to do say honey how is my sweet heart getting along now days my young hammer well you please hand parlies earlier season him a visit for me may I want to see you in something tiny. breakfast & lunch again & hal hammered him in darüber hie a fail now from memory want of brought them reach again because be not getting crazy again. To Young Henry # now rent of young hammer many adrians got to fail Enrolled Jan. 1, 1910 Re-enrolled Sept. 9, 1918. 5-192 BRIEF. A child showing one-sixteenth or less Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, Indian fashion, who, if debarred from the Government schools, could not obtain an education, may be permitted in the reservation day and boarding schools, but it is preferable that it be not transferred to a nonreservation school, without special permission from the Office. Children showing one-eighth or less Indian blood, whose parents do not live on an Indian reservation, whose home is among white people where there are churches and schools, who are presumed to have adopted the white man's manners and customs, and are to all intents and purposes white people, are debarred from enrollment in the Government nonreservation and reservation schools. Superintendents, in all cases where doubt exists as to the degree of Indian blood of a child proposed for transfer, should fully satisfy themselves of the facts by affidavits from reliable persons, which affidavits must be kept on file at the school. A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both Superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and Superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. A pupil dismissed from school for cause must not be enrolled in any other school without the permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Full facts must be submitted with each request. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Oct. 11, 1918. Mr. Charlie Frank, Potlatch, Washington. Dear Mr. Frank: Your daughter Annie Frank was arrested at Ellensburg and returned to Cushman. I have talked with her but do not think she appreciates your efforts and mine in her behalf. She acts as though she had done something deserving of credit for her bravery, etc. I am willing to give her again a chance, but as you understand this is not a reform school and we have no place for a thoroughly bad boy, or girl. If Annie refuses her chance, she will be returned to you or sent to the reform school. When you can, I should like you to visit Cushman. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Oct. 1, 1918. Mr. William C. Miller, Potlatch, Washington. Dear Mr. Miller: Please deliver the enclosed letter to Mr. Frank. His daughter came to school with Mrs. Hade and her children but she ran away last Saturday night with Edith Cawker. Please advise Mr. Frank that his two children must be kept in school. If he is wise, he would return them at once without delay. Willie ran away with Levi Blade on Friday night last. The girl is inclined to be foolish and is being talked about in letters from her friends as the enclosed letter shows. If she remains on the reservation, she will be ruined. Unless these children are returned promptly to Cushman, I shall take legal steps to have them placed in school, as I can not have such a girl running around loose on the reservation. Very respectfully, Superintendent Union City, Wash. Sept. 16, 1918. Miss Sweet Williams: My Dearest loving Sweet Williams: I am going to drop you a few lines to ask you how you are dearie. Hope you are fine and dandy as ever, so am I, Honey dear. I wish I was in your pocket right now. What you say, I go over there, you were gone already and I knew it. Gee, I felt so bad to not see you dear, well my dearest Sweet Williams, I never once thought you would leave dear old Skokomish but see it, I wish I was with you. I may reach there yet Dearie, I shall try and get away somehow Miss Ross wants me to go to school here. See me marched up to the fair ground from the High School. But I wish I was there Saturday nights; wouldn't that be nice tho, Oh gash, I wish. Say do you see Freddie Miller Saturday evenings.. Well Annie the people over here is having trouble over Clarence now, he has Eliza Allen, they just came back from Quilcene last night, and he was telling around he got the best of you tho when he had you for a ride Sunday night. Well, I must close now. My best regards to all. So Good bye, answer soon. Dorothy Purdy From Miss Pansy RECORD OF PUPIL IN SCHOOL Record of Annie Frank at Cushman School.
